title: Deep Learning Scaling is Predictable, Empirically
summary: Across machine translation, language modelling, image classification and speech recognition, generalization error falls as a power law of training-set size. Model size needed to fit the data also grows as a power law of data size.
key_claims: Generalization error follows a power law in training data size across several domains.
The exponent depends on the task domain, and is less sensitive to model architecture.
Learning curves have a small-data region, a power-law region, and an irreducible-error region.

title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
summary: Language-model cross-entropy loss follows smooth power laws in model size (non-embedding parameters), dataset size and training compute, over more than seven orders of magnitude. Architectural details such as depth versus width matter little within a wide range.
key_claims: Loss scales as a power law in parameters, data and compute when the other two are not a bottleneck.
Larger models are more sample-efficient: they reach the same loss with fewer tokens.
For a fixed compute budget, the paper recommended growing model size faster than dataset size and stopping training before convergence.

title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (Chinchilla)
summary: For a fixed compute budget, model size and number of training tokens should be scaled in roughly equal proportion. Chinchilla (70B parameters, about 1.4 trillion tokens) outperformed the 280B-parameter Gopher trained with the same compute.
key_claims: Parameters and training tokens should grow roughly equally as compute grows.
A rule of thumb that follows is about 20 training tokens per parameter.
Many large models of the time (such as Gopher and GPT-3) were undertrained for their size.

title: Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models
summary: Some abilities are near random in smaller models and then appear sharply in larger ones, so they cannot be predicted by extrapolating small-model performance. Examples include multi-step arithmetic in few-shot prompting and the benefit of chain-of-thought prompting.
key_claims: An ability is called emergent if it is absent in smaller models but present in larger ones.
Emergent abilities are not predictable by simple extrapolation from smaller scales.
Prompting techniques such as chain-of-thought only help beyond a certain model scale.

title: Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?
summary: Apparent emergent abilities can be produced by the choice of metric. Nonlinear or discontinuous metrics such as exact-match accuracy turn smooth underlying improvement into a sudden jump; with continuous metrics, performance improves smoothly and predictably with scale.
key_claims: Sharp jumps often come from all-or-nothing metrics, not from sudden changes in the model.
Switching to continuous metrics (such as token edit distance) shows smooth improvement.
Claims of emergence should be checked against the metric and the number of models evaluated.

title: Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models
summary: When unique text runs out, repeating data helps up to a point. Training for up to about four epochs on repeated data is nearly as good as using unique data; beyond that, the value of extra repeated tokens decays towards zero.
key_claims: Up to about 4 epochs of repetition costs very little compared with unique data.
With many more repetitions, adding compute stops helping.
Mixing in code data or relaxing quality filters are ways to stretch a limited text budget.

title: Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal: Accounting for Inference in Language Model Scaling Laws
summary: Chinchilla-optimal training ignores the cost of serving the model. When a model will serve many inference requests, the total cost is lower if you train a smaller model on more tokens than the Chinchilla ratio suggests.
key_claims: Total lifetime cost includes training and inference compute.
With high expected inference demand, smaller models trained longer are cheaper overall.
This helps explain why recent models are often trained far past 20 tokens per parameter.

title: GPT-4 Technical Report
summary: The report describes infrastructure built to scale predictably. GPT-4's final loss, and its pass rate on a subset of a coding benchmark (HumanEval), were predicted in advance from much smaller runs using up to 1,000 to 10,000 times less compute.
key_claims: Final training loss was predicted from small runs with a fitted power law.
Some capability metrics could also be forecast from small-scale runs.
Not every capability was predictable; some tasks showed unexpected trends.

title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
summary: Spending more compute at inference time, for example on sequential revisions or search guided by a verifier, can improve answers. Allocating that compute adaptively by question difficulty was more than four times more efficient than a best-of-N baseline, and on easier and medium questions a smaller model with extra test-time compute could beat a much larger model.
key_claims: Test-time compute is a second scaling axis besides parameters and training data.
The best way to spend test-time compute depends on the difficulty of the question.
For the hardest questions, scaling pretraining was still more effective.
